doc.title: Allan Vaché interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Jazz on the radio, smooth jazz and WUCF
summary: More jazz on public radio; he rejects smooth jazz as lacking swing and praises Orlando station WUCF.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: The state of jazz on the radio, and stuff that’s coming out currently, does it affect your own playing much? Do you listen to the contemporary young guys playing?

Yes, constantly. And I will say that there seems to be more jazz on the radio now than there was say ten years ago. But most of the stations are public radio stations or college stations and so forth. In Orlando we have WUCF which is an excellent jazz station. Now it depends on what you’re talking about. If you’re talking about the stuff that they call smooth jazz, no, I don’t listen to that stuff at all. I don’t consider that jazz, I consider that a kind of a smooth form of rock & roll. Because I don’t know who said it, but to me if a player does not have a natural sense of swing in his playing, if the phrasing isn’t swinging, then it’s not worth listening to as a jazz player. And all the great players, no matter where they went in an extension, I mean from Parker to Coltrane to Coleman, Ornette Coleman or any of these guys, even though how far they extended their improvisation, everything still swung its ass off. I mean Coltrane could swing like a mother. And he did constantly. It may not be necessarily the way I would think or somebody else would think because he was constantly innovative and creating new things. But he was still always swinging. And that stuff, like let’s face it, Kenny G can’t swing his way out of a paper bag, we all know it, everybody knows it. But that’s not what those people are listening for. They’re listening to — nice background music while you’re lighting candles at dinner. But the other stations, the public radio stations, college stations, like WUCF in Orlando that I listen to constantly, I have it on my car radio all the time, and they’re nice. They play some of my records, they play a lot of local artists there, there’s some really good players from the Orlando area, John Allred, a wonderful trombone player, and a few others. And we all have recorded. They play a lot of local artists plus they play a lot of national things. And within the spectrum of a very good — a very long spectrum of music, from classic and traditional all the way up to super- contemporary things that are going on today. It’s worth listening to. Not everything I enjoy, but I like the idea that these guys are willing to take a chance and play the whole entire spectrum, instead of saying well we’re not going to play anything that was done before 1950, which a lot of places do, a lot of stations do.
